title: Why Avoid Division: The Hardware Motivation for Stein's Algorithm
content: On binary computers, integer division is a slow multi-cycle operation, while right-shift (halving) and subtraction are O(1) single-cycle instructions. Stein's algorithm (1967) replaces every modular reduction step in Euclid's algorithm with a subtraction and at least one halving, guaranteeing geometric decrease of a+b. This makes the binary GCD roughly twice as fast as Euclid on hardware without a hardware divider — microcontrollers, FPGAs, and cryptographic co-processors. The algorithm actually predates Stein: it appears in Chinese mathematics circa 1st century BCE, but Stein's 1967 FORTRAN paper gave the first rigorous modern analysis and complexity bound.
mathContext: Euclid: $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$ — one division per step. Stein: only $\div 2$ (right-shift) and subtraction. Complexity: $O(\log^2(\max(a,b)))$ bit operations vs $O(\log(\max(a,b)))$ divisions for Euclid.

title: Eight GCD Helper Lemmas: The Mathematical Backbone
content: The eight private lemmas encode the key mathematical facts for each algorithm branch. `gcd_double_double` uses Nat.gcd_mul_left directly. `gcd_two_mul_of_odd` uses the coprimality argument: if b is odd, gcd(2,b)=1, so gcd(2a,b) = gcd(a,b) via Nat.Coprime.gcd_mul_left_cancel. `gcd_sub_right` reduces to gcd_rec (which says gcd(a,b) = gcd(a, b mod a)) after showing (b−a) mod a = b mod a via mod_sub_self. `gcd_odd_sub_half` chains gcd_of_odd_two_mul + gcd_sub_right: when both a,b are odd, b−a is even, so gcd(a,(b−a)/2) = gcd(a,2·((b−a)/2)) = gcd(a,b−a) = gcd(a,b).
mathContext: $\gcd(2a, 2b) = 2\gcd(a,b)$. If $b$ odd: $\gcd(2a,b) = \gcd(a,b)$ (since $\gcd(2,b)=1$). If $a,b$ odd, $a \leq b$: $\gcd(a, (b-a)/2) = \gcd(a,b)$ (since $b-a$ is even, apply odd-factor removal then subtraction).

title: binaryGcd: Seven Branches, Termination by a+b
content: The definition has seven mutually exclusive branches: (1) a=0 → b; (2) b=0 → a; (3) both even → 2·binaryGcd(a/2,b/2); (4) a even, b odd → binaryGcd(a/2,b); (5) a odd, b even → binaryGcd(a,b/2); (6) both odd, a≤b → binaryGcd(a,(b−a)/2); (7) both odd, a>b → binaryGcd((a−b)/2,b). The `termination_by a + b` and `decreasing_by omega` tell Lean the decreasing measure; omega automatically verifies that each recursive call strictly decreases a+b in all 5 non-base branches.
mathContext: Termination: (3) $\frac{a}{2} + \frac{b}{2} < a + b$; (4,5) one argument halves; (6) $a + \frac{b-a}{2} = \frac{a+b}{2} < a+b$; (7) symmetric.

title: binaryGcd_eq_gcd: Correctness by Well-Founded Induction
content: The proof of `binaryGcd_eq_gcd` mirrors the algorithm's structure: unfold `binaryGcd`, apply `split_ifs` to expose all seven branches, then for each recursive branch apply the IH and the corresponding helper lemma. For example, in the both-even branch: rw IH for (a/2,b/2), then rewrite a = 2*(a/2) and b = 2*(b/2), and apply gcd_double_double symmetrically. The termination proof obligation is automatically discharged by `omega` in all branches. The symmetry of the argument structure (the same `termination_by a + b` appears in both the definition and the induction proof) is what makes the proof mechanically straightforward.
mathContext: For each branch, the IH gives binaryGcd(x,y) = Nat.gcd(x,y) for smaller arguments. Then the helper lemma (e.g., $\gcd(a/2, b/2) = \gcd(a,b)/2$ → $2\cdot\gcd(a/2,b/2) = \gcd(a,b)$) closes the goal.

title: GCD Properties: All Follow Immediately from Correctness
content: Once `binaryGcd_eq_gcd` is established, all four GCD properties are trivial one-liners: `binaryGcd_comm` rewrites via binaryGcd_eq_gcd and applies Nat.gcd_comm. `binaryGcd_dvd_left` and `binaryGcd_dvd_right` rewrite and apply the corresponding Mathlib lemmas. `dvd_binaryGcd` rewrites and applies Nat.dvd_gcd. This pattern — prove correctness once, then inherit all properties by reduction — is a fundamental proof-engineering principle in formal mathematics.
mathContext: $\text{binaryGcd}(a,b) = \text{Nat.gcd}(a,b) \Rightarrow$ all GCD properties transfer: $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b,a)$, $\gcd(a,b) \mid a$, $\gcd(a,b) \mid b$, $k \mid a \land k \mid b \Rightarrow k \mid \gcd(a,b)$.

title: Bézout Corollary and Computational Verification
content: `bezout_via_binaryGcd` first rewrites binaryGcd a b as Nat.gcd a b (via binaryGcd_eq_gcd), then applies Int.gcd_eq_gcd_ab to obtain the Bézout coefficients Int.gcdA and Int.gcdB. The cast `(Nat.gcd a b : ℤ) = ↑(Int.gcd (a:ℤ) (b:ℤ))` is the only non-trivial step. The five `native_decide` examples verify the algorithm on concrete inputs: gcd(12,8)=4, gcd(35,15)=5, gcd(17,5)=1, gcd(252,198)=18, gcd(1071,462) matches Nat.gcd. These use kernel evaluation rather than proof, confirming that the definition computes correctly at runtime.
mathContext: $\exists x, y \in \mathbb{Z}: \gcd(a,b) = ax + by$ (Bézout's lemma). After $\text{binaryGcd}(a,b) = \text{Nat.gcd}(a,b)$, use $\text{Int.gcd\_eq\_gcd\_ab}$: $\text{Int.gcd}(a,b) = a \cdot \text{gcdA}(a,b) + b \cdot \text{gcdB}(a,b)$.
